title: Mastering the Post-Trabeculectomy Crisis: High IOP Management
summary: The early post-operative period after trabeculectomy is a critical window where surgical success is determined. This guide provides a comprehensive framework for diagnosing and managing elevated Intraocular Pressure (IOP) in the freshly operated eye.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Trabeculectomy remains the 'gold standard' for surgical glaucoma management. A 'fresh' trabeculectomy (Days 1–14) requires meticulous monitoring. Failure to achieve the target IOP in this phase often indicates a mechanical or physiological blockage of the newly created drainage pathway. Early intervention is paramount to prevent bleb failure and irreversible glaucomatous damage.

sections.title: The Post-Op Exam Checklist
content: Visual Acuity: Rule out 'wipe-out' syndrome or macular serous detachment.
IOP Measurement: Goldmann Applanation (avoid excessive pressure) or Tonopen.
Bleb Morphology: Assess height (elevated vs. flat), extent (diffuse vs. localized), and vascularity (corkscrew vessels).
Seidel Test: Use 2% Fluorescein to check for wound or bleb leaks.
Anterior Chamber Depth: Grade using Van Herick or Shaffer (Peripheral vs. Central depth).
Internal Ostium: Gonioscopic view of the sclerostomy site (if safe/view allows).
Fundoscopy: Rule out choroidal effusions or suprachoroidal hemorrhage.

branches: Obstruction of Internal Ostium (Blood, Fibrin, Iris, Vitreous)

sections.title: Emergency Red Flags (High IOP + Shallow AC)
content: Malignant Glaucoma (Ciliary Block): High IOP, Shallow AC, no choroidals.
Suprachoroidal Hemorrhage: Sudden pain, loss of vision, high IOP, dark fundus mass.
Pupillary Block: High IOP, iris bombe, usually due to absent/blocked iridectomy.
Incarceration of Vitreous: Blockage of the ostium by vitreous wick.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup & Investigations
content: 1. Gonioscopy: Vital to see if iris or blood is plugging the ostium.
2. B-Scan Ultrasound: Crucial if the media is hazy to rule out Suprachoroidal Hemorrhage.
3. AS-OCT: Visualizes the scleral flap, subconjunctival space, and ostium patency.
4. UBM: Detailed view of the ciliary body position in suspected Malignant Glaucoma.

sections.title: Management: The Step-by-Step Protocol
content: Step 1: Digital Ocular Massage (Allen-Burian Maneuver) to force fluid through the flap.
Step 2: Laser Suture Lysis (LSL) if sutures are too tight (use Hoskins lens).
Step 3: Medical Therapy (Aqueous suppressants, but avoid miotics if malignant glaucoma is suspected).
Step 4: Atropine 1% for Malignant Glaucoma or Pupillary Block.
Step 5: AC Reformation or Surgical Revision if mechanical blockage persists.

sections.title: Clinical Pearl: The Scleral Flap
content: Suture tension is a balance: Too tight = High IOP; Too loose = Hypotony/Flat AC.
Always place adjustable or releasable sutures if you anticipate a high risk of failure.
Check for 'Overhang' of the bleb, which may indicate posterior flow.

content.explanation: B: Bleb (Height/Vascularity), I: Inflammation (AC cells), G: Gonioscopy (Ostium), H: Hemorrhage (Choroidal), E: Effusion, L: Leak (Seidel), P: Pressure (IOP).

sections.title: Specific Surgical Obstructions
content: Blood/Fibrin: Can be cleared with Intracameral TPA (25 micrograms).
Iris Incarceration: Requires surgical repositioning or YAG PI if localized.
Vitreous: Requires anterior vitrectomy to clear the ostium.
Tenon's Cyst: Requires needling with MMC or 5-FU.

sections.title: Malignant Glaucoma Management
content: 1. Cycloplegia: Immediate Atropine 1% TID to pull the ciliary body back.
2. Aqueous Suppressants: IV Mannitol, Oral Acetazolamide, Timolol.
3. YAG Capsulotomy/Hyaloidotomy: To break the aqueous misdirection.
4. Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV): With 'Zonulo-hyaloido-vitrectomy' if medical therapy fails.

rows: Monitor for steroid-induced IOP spike (weeks later)
Avoid in very wide angles unless necessary

sections.title: Prognosis & Landmarks
content: TVT Study (Tube vs Trab): Trabeculectomy with MMC remains effective but has higher early complication rates than tubes.
Early high IOP is a significant predictor of long-term surgical failure if not addressed within the first 14 days.
Encapsulated blebs (Tenon's cyst) often respond well to needling with an 80% success rate if performed early.
